analysis.one_liner: Restores strict Federal Reserve oversight for banks holding $50 billion to $250 billion in assets.
analysis.headline: A bill to restore stricter oversight of midsize banks, introduced days after the Silicon Valley Bank collapse, died in committee with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo a 2018 law that exempted banks with $50 billion to $250 billion in assets from the strictest Federal Reserve oversight. It would lower the thresholds that trigger mandatory stress tests, leverage limits, and liquidity requirements, so more banks would have to prove they could survive a financial shock. It was introduced days after the Silicon Valley Bank collapse in March 2023 and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Depositors at midsize banks benefit from stronger cushions and closer supervision that make bank failures less likely. Taxpayers and the deposit insurance fund benefit too, because when a bank fails, the FDIC's cleanup costs ultimately feed into what ordinary bank customers and taxpayers bear.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would restore the pre-2018 threshold, requiring banks with $50 billion or more in assets to meet enhanced Federal Reserve standards — stress testing, leverage limits, liquidity requirements, and resolution plans — rather than leaving banks between $100 billion and $250 billion to the Fed's discretion.

It would require company-run stress tests starting at $10 billion in assets, performed annually or semiannually, and mandate risk committees at banks of $10 billion or more, catching weakness earlier at more institutions.

The stated purpose, per the bill's title and timing, was to stabilize banks like those that failed or were seized in March 2023, protecting depositors and the deposit insurance fund from repeat failures.

analysis.who_pays: Banks with assets between $10 billion and $250 billion pay the cost: they would face mandatory Fed stress testing, leverage limits, liquidity requirements, resolution ("living will") plans, and internal risk committees, with compliance staff and systems they currently avoid. Those costs can be passed on to borrowers and savers through fees and loan pricing.

drawbacks.text: The added compliance burden falls on banks between $10 billion and $250 billion in assets, and those costs can be passed to customers through higher fees and tighter lending, an objection banks raised when the 2018 exemption was created in the first place.

Stricter standards are not a guarantee: Silicon Valley Bank failed despite operating under some supervisory requirements, so the bill's title promised more stabilization than any single rule change can deliver.

The bill was a one-page repeal of the 2018 exemption rather than a redesigned supervisory framework, leaving open questions about whether the pre-2018 rules were the right calibration for banks in the $50-$100 billion range.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the public, the upside is real but indirect: tougher standards at midsize banks reduce the odds of the kind of failures that hit depositors and the FDIC insurance fund in 2023. The costs are compliance expenses at banks holding $10 billion to $250 billion, some share of which would reach borrowers and savers. A genuine weakness is that the bill was a blunt repeal of one section of the 2018 law rather than a tailored fix, and no supervisory rule fully prevents bank failure. Still, the core trade — more oversight of midsize banks in exchange for higher compliance costs — weighed toward the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 14, 2023, four days after Silicon Valley Bank's failure, and was referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor during the entire Congress.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Midsize and regional banks are better off, because they continue to avoid the stricter capital, liquidity, and testing requirements the bill would have imposed. Depositors gained nothing from the bill's death beyond what existing rules already provide.

for.name: Seth Moulton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it died in committee with zero cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: House Committee on Financial Services (Chair: Patrick McHenry)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after receiving the referral: no hearings, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member signed on, so the fight never took a partisan shape; the sponsor was a Democrat and the House committee that controlled the bill's fate was run by Republicans.

industries.industry: Regional and midsize banks ($50-$250 billion in assets)
industries.note: These banks gained the 2018 exemption this bill would have repealed; losing it means mandatory stress testing, leverage limits, and liquidity requirements. Their interest in keeping the lighter rules runs against the bill's aim of fewer bank failures.
The bill would lower the company-run stress test threshold to $10 billion and require annual or semiannual testing, adding compliance work for banks well below the regional-bank tier.
